title: Anticipatory KV slab ledger and tenant-priority watermarking for GPU memory headroom
creator: Amina Patel
description:
Background: As mixed-tenant inference traffic grows we increasingly see tight headroom windows on GPUs where weights+KV+activations compete for a limited pool. Current soft-quotas and global KV trimming cause noisy eviction storms and p99 latency spikes for premium tenants during microbursts. Goal: Introduce a per-GPU slab ledger that tracks KV occupancy by slab segment, maintain anticipatory headroom envelopes (probabilistic) per tenant/model, and surface tenant-priority watermarks that bias eviction/compression decisions. This should reduce OOMs and unexpected late evictions while preserving latency SLOs for high-priority workloads.

Scope: Design and implement the slab ledger data model, headroom envelope estimator, priority-weighted eviction policy, and an operator-visible dashboard. Integrate with continuous-batching so that activation budget forecasts are coordinated with KV reservations. Provide a canary rollout path and A/B comparison against the current soft-quota policy.

Core approach:
- Ledger: map KV allocations to discrete slab segments (4–16MB) tagged with tenant, model-version, and recency score. Ledger stores current slab occupancy and per-slab compression state.
- Headroom estimator: maintain a rolling window (configurable; default 10m) of per-tenant KV occupancy samples and request activation envelopes. Compute probabilistic headroom envelope H_t = mu + z* sigma + gamma * p95_burst where z derived from target tail (default z=2.33 for 1% tail), gamma tuned from microburst tests.
- Priority watermarking: each tenant receives a dynamic watermark derived from their SLA tier and current H_t. Watermarks map to eviction lanes: protected (no eviction unless > watermark+grace), compress-only, and preemptible.
- Eviction policy: prefer cross-tenant compaction first for slabs in compress-only lane, then reassign preemptible slabs. Avoid immediate weight offload unless headroom < critical threshold.
- Activation coordination: continuous-batcher will expose predicted activation memory per request (based on batch size distribution and seq length), and the estimator will reserve transient headroom for predicted activations for the next 30s window.

Acceptance criteria:
- Reduce per-GPU OOM events by >= 70% in mixed-tenant load tests (50/30/20 high/medium/low priority split).
- Maintain p99 tail latency within 1.2x of baseline for protected tenants during bursts.
- Reduce eviction-induced request retries by >= 60%.
- Dashboard exposes per-tenant slab occupancy, headroom envelope, eviction lane counts, and savings estimate.

Trade-offs and open questions:
- Complexity vs benefit: slab ledger increases bookkeeping and slightly more CPU on the host. We accept added host CPU for fewer OOMs, but need to quantify.
- Compression overhead: compressing slabs trades GPU memory for CPU cycles and possible latency; we'll prefer GPU-friendly compression codecs and limit background compaction to low-load windows.
- Fairness: priority watermarking intentionally biases evictions; need explicit guardrails for long-running fairness (slab aging).

Plan and milestones:
- Week 1: Design doc + data model + simulation harness (Amina)
- Week 2: Implement ledger and estimator prototype + unit tests (Jorge)
